A particle accelerator near Amman in Jordan, opened in 2017, that is run jointly by governments of the Middle East, among them rivals such as Israel, Iran, the Palestinian Authority and Turkey.

A synchrotron speeds electrons round a ring until they give off very bright light, from infrared to X-rays. Scientists use it to study the structure of materials, proteins, ancient objects and much else. Before SESAME, researchers in the region had to travel to Europe or elsewhere for this.

The project was modelled on CERN, the European physics laboratory founded after World War II partly to bring former enemies together. Under the wing of UNESCO, parts of an old German synchrotron were donated and shipped to Jordan in 2002, and the machine was built up over fifteen years. It runs on electricity from its own solar plant.

Its members are Cyprus, Egypt, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Pakistan, Palestine and Turkey, a mix seldom found around one table. It is an experiment in whether science can work where politics fails.
